title: 2 Samuel 8:15–18
context: 2 Samuel 8:15–18 closes the summary of David’s reign with a statement about his just rule and a list of his chief officials: Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, Seraiah as scribe, Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites, and David’s sons as “chief ministers.” The list shows the organization of David’s kingdom at its height. A parallel list appears in 1 Chronicles 18:14–17, which differs in some names and in how it describes David’s sons.

verses.text: David reigned over all Israel; and David executed justice and righteousness for all his people.
verses.arminianNotes: “David reigned over all Israel; and David executed justice and righteousness for all his people.” Arminian readers note that the ideal of kingship is just rule for the good of the people. David’s reign at this point models what God intended for Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “justice and righteousness” are the marks of the messianic king, whose reign Isaiah describes as upholding David’s kingdom “with justice and with righteousness” (Isaiah 9:7). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing David at his best, and both see it pointing to the perfectly just reign of Christ.

verses.text: Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder,
verses.arminianNotes: Joab the son of Zeruiah is over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud is recorder. Arminian readers note that the list introduces the officials who carry out the king’s rule. Joab in particular will play a major and sometimes troubling role in later chapters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the organization of the kingdom reflects God’s blessing in giving Israel stable government. The recorder likely kept official records, though the exact duties are not described here. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical background, and neither finds a theological dispute in it.

verses.text: Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, Seraiah was scribe,
verses.arminianNotes: Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar are priests, and Seraiah is scribe. Arminian readers note that the list includes priests alongside civil officials, showing the place of worship in David’s kingdom. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:16 reads “Abimelech” and names the scribe Shavsha.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Zadok’s line will become prominent in later priestly history. The relationship between Ahimelech and Abiathar here and elsewhere in Samuel is not explained in this verse, and readers should not overstate what the text says. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical background and note the parallel’s different names plainly.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David’s sons were chief ministers.
verses.arminianNotes: Benaiah is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, “and David’s sons were chief ministers.” Arminian readers note that David’s sons hold high positions in the royal court. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 18:17 describes them as “chief officials serving the king.” The difference in wording is noted plainly here without trying to settle it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Cherethites and Pelethites appear to be a royal guard under Benaiah, who will later serve Solomon. The precise role of David’s sons is described differently in the two parallel lists. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing the summary of David’s officials, and both caution against reading more into the titles than the text states.
